title: Sopaka's cremation ground
hookLine: a boy abandoned in a charnel ground is found by the Buddha (Theragatha, Sopaka)

cards: A cremation ground at night is no place for anyone, least of all a child. The commentaries on the elder monks' verses tell two stories under the name Sopaka, and they don't match.
In one, a relative who was angry with a boy took him there, tied him down beside a body, and left. In the other, a boy was born there, after his mother was taken for dead.
Some scholars think these are two different monks who shared a name. In both, the Buddha comes to the child. Today, the boy who was found.

teach.b: First, the rescue. In the telling with the relative, the boy, bound and afraid, calls out in the dark.

The Buddha, far away, sees him, and the story says light reaches him, the bonds fall away, and he's brought to the Buddha. The tradition tells it as a wonder, and it's told that way here. Second, the verses.

In the Theragatha, the lines under the name Sopaka are quieter. He saw the Buddha walking in the shade of a building, he says. He went up, arranged his robe over one shoulder, bowed, and walked behind him.
Then the Buddha asks him questions, and Sopaka answers without fear. The Buddha is pleased, and with a few words of welcome, receives him into the order.
Later tradition connects him with a short set of questions and answers for a young novice, which begins: what is one? All beings live by food. Fourth, what the story keeps doing.
The details shift from telling to telling, but the shape holds. A child left alone in the dark is seen. He's not lectured.
He's asked questions, and listened to, and his answers are taken seriously.
He's given a place, a teacher, and a community to belong to. The cremation ground is where his story begins, not where it ends.

how: In Theravada countries children can be ordained as novices, and the short set of novice's questions linked to Sopaka is chanted and learned in monasteries as part of the Khuddakapatha.

o: a forest hut where monks sit alone
a temple where children learn verses
a cremation ground, where bodies burn

p: where the boy was left at night

s: every telling agrees on how Sopaka came to the cremation ground
the commentaries tell two stories, left there by an angry relative or born there, and some scholars think they're about two monks.
in his verses, Sopaka answers the Buddha's questions without fear
and the Buddha, pleased, receives him into the order.
Sopaka was turned away for being too young
the Buddha welcomed him into the order.

games.q: you're the Buddha. far away, at night, a boy has been left alone in a cremation ground. what does the story have you do?
o: send word to his family in the morning.
reach him, and bring him to safety.
wait and see if someone else comes.
games.why: in the commentary the Buddha sees him in the dark, the bonds fall away, and the boy is brought to him. later he's questioned kindly and welcomed into the order.

practice: Hold one child in mind: in your family, on your street, at a school you know, or the child you once were. Ask one plain question: what would help them be a little safer, a little more heard?
If nothing comes, simply wish them well, and let the question rest.

wordCard.voice: Susana, a cremation ground. Where a boy left alone at night was found, questioned kindly, and welcomed by the Buddha. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali susana: a cremation ground, where bodies were burned or left; where Sopaka's story begins.

carryVoice: Your line: found. The child in the dark was asked, and listened to. See you tomorrow.
